item.title: Americans’ Guilty Spending Reflects a Rational Approach to Joy and Risk
item.description: Americans like to spend money, and they’re good at it. But they also feel kind of bad about it.
item.dc:creator: Allison Schrager

item.title: Hugging Face Hack: Don't Let Dwarkesh Patel's AI Language Fool You
item.description: The attacks on Hugging Face ran from May to late July, yet the details of what actually happened when OpenAI’s artificial-intelligence agents deceived their human overseers and breached the online repository of AI models and datasets are still trickling out.
item.dc:creator: Parmy Olson

item.title: US Shouldn't Cut Off Asia Allies to Make Peace With North Korea
item.description: With typical bombast, the White House seems to be shifting strategy on the long-frozen conflict on the Korean Peninsula. Unfortunately, it’s moving in the wrong direction.
item.dc:creator: The Editors

item.title: Supreme Court Ballroom Ruling Erodes the Rule of Law
item.description: In a genuinely surprising decision, the Supreme Court has dismissed a lawsuit against President Donald Trump’s congressionally unauthorized ballroom construction project. Over a dissent by Chief Justice John Roberts, who was joined by the court’s three liberals, the court’s five conservatives said that the National Trust for Historic Preservation lacked standing to challenge the ballroom being built where the East Wing of the White House used to be.
item.dc:creator: Noah Feldman

item.title: The ‘SaaSpocalypse’ Has a Remarkable Number of Survivors
item.description: You may remember February’s run on software-as-a-service stocks in which billions of dollars in value were wiped off companies that investors worried would be obliterated by artificial intelligence in the not-too-distant future, their specialist features replaced by bespoke in-house tools built on demand by AI instead.
item.dc:creator: Dave Lee

item.title: Tactical Nukes Are a Gateway Drug to Armageddon
item.description: The US is quietly — and largely with a view to a potential war against China — tweaking its nuclear strategy, contemplating a bigger role for so-called tactical nukes. To the uninitiated, the shift may seem arcane. To those in the know, the stakes are nothing less than the risk of atomic Armageddon.
item.dc:creator: Andreas Kluth

item.title: Aston Martin Should Lift the Debt Hood for Bondholders
item.description: The company that makes Aston Martin’s iconic sportscars has infuriated its bondholders by taking on more debt, allegedly reassigning assets to new creditors and saying almost nothing about the potentially nasty side effects for its existing backers. The automaker may well have done nothing wrong. But its studied reticence is hard to justify.
item.dc:creator: Chris Hughes

item.title: Nintendo Can Use Nostalgia to Compete With Grand Theft Auto VI
item.description: In early March, Nintendo Co. released Pokémon Pokopia, the latest instalment in one of the world’s most prolific video-game franchises. I’d pre-ordered the game to arrive on launch day, eager to play something that promised to combine the cosy, world-building mechanics of its Animal Crossing: New Horizons with the pocket-sized monsters I’d grown up with. item.dc:creator: Emily Nicolle

item.title: Deepfakes and AI Slop Are Supercharging Misleading Political Ads
item.description: In this depressing era of AI slop, psyops and deepfakes in politics, is it wrong to yearn for simpler times?
item.dc:creator: Jessica Karl

item.title: India’s Youth Are Angry. Its Billionaires Are at War
item.description: India’s rich are just as furious as its working class, but their anger flows in opposite directions. While the “cockroach” movement grew from college students demanding fair exams to schoolchildren protesting broken roads — all training their ire on Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s government — the corporate elite have turned their knives on each other.
item.dc:creator: Andy Mukherjee

item.title: Amazon Charged the First Price
item.description: Vickrey auctions, a GoPro meme merger and Kalshi gamblers.
item.dc:creator: Matt Levine

item.title: Banning Kids From Social Media Is Only Half a Solution
item.description: Australia’s world-leading efforts to keep youth off social media are a closely watched experiment that more than two dozen countries are now trying to imitate. But the early data suggests it’s not going very well.
item.dc:creator: Catherine Thorbecke

item.title: The Grand Canyon Floods Point to Our Bigger Water Crisis
item.description: The reason most lottery winners eventually go broke is that they aren’t prepared for the unexpected influx of wealth. They blow it on luxuries, bad investments and long-lost relatives. Dry places face a similar risk when they receive a sudden deluge of rainfall. If they’re not ready to capture and use it, then the water can do more harm than good.
item.dc:creator: Mark Gongloff
